title: FilmNation CEO Glen Basner Talks Art Of Film Sales & Financing: “It’s Really Just About Sitting & Listening To The Filmmaking Team” – Zurich Summit
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Backrooms’ Director Kane Parsons Says: “I Don’t View It As A Horror Project” – Zurich Summit Tales Of Syria’s Disappeared; Lebanese Wartime Adoption & Palestinian Mental Health Set For Cinemed-Aflamuna Project Incubator Netflix-Acquired Animation ‘In Waves’ To Open The American French Film Festival In L.A. View All September 27, 2026 6:59am Glen Basner at 22nd Zurich Film Festival Getty Images for ZFF FilmNation Entertainment Founder and CEO Glen Basner will receive the Game Changer Award this evening at the Zurich Summit , the annual industry event aimed at fostering transatlantic connections taking place within the Zurich Film Festival. As part of the honor, Basner participated in an onstage conversation on Saturday moderated by German Oscar-winning director Edward Berger . Over the course of an hour, the pair dug into Basner’s trajectory from sales rep at his father’s garment business, to heading up one of the world’s top international indie sales, financing and production companies. Related Stories News Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises -- Zurich Summit News "I Can Promise You, We Had No Idea That 'Obsession' Was Going To Become 'Obsession'", Says Hit Horror Film's Seller -- Zurich Summit Basner and Berger go back a long way, having first met at the beginning of their film careers in the early 1990s at famed New York production company Good Machine. Watch on Deadline Basner arrived there from a five-year stint selling ladies knitted sweaters. He had been bitten by the movie bug while helping childhood friend Edward Burns in his spare time on his first film The Brothers McMullen. Burns then invited Basner onto his second feature She’s The One , which was produced by Good Machine. The rest is history. Berger spent a year and a half at the company from 1994, where his paths crossed with Basner. They have stayed connected ever since, with the pair joining forces professionally again on Berger’s 2024 $100M global box office and streaming hit Conclave . “32 years later, it’s such a full circle moment,” said Berger as they kicked off the conversation. Looking back at his time working with Ted Hope, James Schamus and David Linde at Good Machine, Basner said the lessons he learned there had carried him through his career. “I was taught that you could sell movies around the world and not lie to people… that you can value and appreciate the relationships that you develop around the world and treat people not just as if you’re selling them a product, but that you are really delivering them a work of art, and that you’re there to help support them as they go and release the films country by country,” he said. Berger suggested working there had also taught them resilience, recalling how just prior to their arrival, the company had nearly gone bankrupt after it wrapped Ang Lee’s romantic comedy The Wedding Banquet . “It taught us to go through hard times and get stronger… around the time of The Wedding Banquet, the company was basically bankrupt… they decided let’s cancel the photocopier and scrape every last bit together and go to Berlin,” said the director. The film went on to win the Berlinale’s Golden Bear and then took off at the box office to gross some $23M, against the $1M budget, making it the most profitable U.S. film of 1993. After subsequent stints heading up sales at Focus and then The Weinstein Company, Basner created FilmNation in 2008, initially uniquely as a sales company. He said creating his own company had been a natural move for him given his family background. “My father had his own business, and I wanted to be like my father, so I always had this entrepreneurial bug that I wanted to go out and sort of really test my mettle by being on my own and developing something and seeing if it could succeed,” he said. “So that was something I thought about since the first day that I started working in film.” Eighteen years later, the company has expanded organically into finance, production and TV, with bases in New York and L.A., and string of award-winning features in its filmography including The Big Sick , Promising Young Woman, Anora , Conclave , Maria and upcoming pictures Bunker , Talent for Murder and I Play Rocky to name but a few. “The opportunity was clear in 2008. In those days, there were only two strong and dominant, excellent American international sales companies that were unaffiliated with U.S. distribution,” said Basner. “Pretty much at the same time, they both became U.S. distributors. Summit, which was run by Patrick Wachberger, became a U.S. distributor, and Mandate, Joe Drake’s company, was bought by Lionsgate… so there was this big hole for an American, unaffiliated-with-distribution sales company.” Sales craft Talking about FilmNation’s recent slate, Basner said he had wooed Florian Zeller ahead of getting involved in Bunker . “I told him to his face he was my filmmaker crush of the moment,” he joked. “You said that to me too,” replied Berger in mock disbelief. “I know. It was a different moment,” fired back Basner jovially. He recalled how Zeller had been on the cusp of approaching Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz as FilmNation quietly putting out international sales feelers. “He had said, ‘If they say yes, we’ll move forward. If they don’t do the movie, I don’t think I’m going to do the movie.’ Fortunately, they said yes, and then we just really started the work,” said Basner. The film took a traditional pre-sales route thanks to Zeller’s track-record with Oscar-winner The Father , followed by The Son , it’s A-list cast and a “exquisite” script, with the bulk of the international sales tied up at Cannes in 2025. The U.S. deal to Sony Pictures Classics was sealed in collaboration with CAA Media Finance later on, on the basis of the completed film. “There were distributors that were willing to take the risk. It’s not the easiest thing to say: ‘Here’s the script, here’s the director, here are the actors, and here’s your price’. They don’t really get to sit and have hour-long conversations with the filmmaker to fully understand the movie,” said Basner . “They have to trust us to be able to articulate exactly what the movie is and what the intention is of that filmmaker, so that they can then decide to take the significant risk on a movie like this of pre-buying the film.” Talking about their collaboration on Vatican-set thriller Conclave , revolving around the secretive Vatican process of electing a new Pope, Basner said part of the challenge had been conveying Berger’s vision for the film to buyers. He suggested that on the basis of the screenplay alone – it felt like a story about “a bunch of old men talking in rooms” with a potential $12M to $15M price tag. “But that really wasn’t the movie that you were looking to make… You talked about The Parallax View being a point of reference for you,” said Basner, referring to Alan J. Pakula’s 1974 political thriller. “You talked not just about the architecture of the locations, but the architecture of how you wanted the camera to move and the film to feel… all of a sudden this became a political thriller,” continued Basner. The sales veteran said estimating a value of a film, country by country, came down to a mixture of experience and expertise. “You’re responsible to hit these estimates. And human nature takes over, and sometimes you can get a little bit conservative to make sure that you deliver,’ he said. “What we’ve learned over the years is to trust the business acumen and the marketplace experience that we have, and not be too conservative, but actually just deliver the valuation that we think, and be prepared to stand by it in a real way because it’s our money that we’re investing.” “Part of that is, instead of talking all the time about what the market says and what the market will bear, it’s really about just sitting and listening to the filmmaking team so that you really understand, not what I, Glen Basner, thinks the movie is going to be or should be, but the movie that the filmmaker wants to make.” Basner revealed he was wary of going down the packaging route of attaching known talent when helping get big projects of the ground, suggesting attempts to mitigate risks on films, whether via the cast or other factors, can sometimes lead to less exciting films. “Sometimes we have to take more risk on an unknown actor because they are the best person for that role to make the best version of the movie, and we have to trust that filmmaker to deliver on that, not in a naive way, in a thoughtful way, but really trust that that’s really what’s going to drive the value for that movie,” said Basner. “I really am encouraging everybody to look around, look at what’s working in the marketplace. There are a lot of films that, on paper, did not make sense. The history of our company is predominantly on films that did not make sense to the marketplace at the beginning.” Conclave clash Berger revealed they had not always seen eye-to-eye in the final stages of bringing Conclave to fruition. “After quite a long edit… I was basically done with the film. I’d run out of ideas… I really wanted to go to Venice or at least show them the movie and see if they’d show it,” recalled Berger. “This was in in May. Glenn got on the phone and made me furious. I hated him. He just kind of said, ‘I’m not sure the movie’s ready, don’t rush it…Venice is going to be expensive, and we don’t have American distribution in place’,” he recalled. Lead producer Tessa Ross also felt the movie was “missing something” and after test screenings with friends and family sparked an “ok” response, Berger went back to the edit suite and even reshot one or two scenes. Berger credited Berger and Ross for pushing the extra mile on the film, while his energy levels were low after an arduous months-long edit process. “This is going back to Good Machine, and what I took from Good Machine… which was you can always do better… whether its budget, contract or the cut of the movie,” said Berger. “We just edited and edited and edited and made the music again and revised it, and finally something cracked… little things, just shifted and gave us the confidence that the movie was ready. But it was really half a year later.” Organic expansion Taking stock of FilmNation’s trajectory since 2008, Basner said the expansion into production and TV had been organic. “We never really anticipated becoming the company that we have over time, but things changed. One, as we continued to do our jobs and have success, we gained confidence through experience, and we were ready to do things like fund our own films,” he said. A second development was the convergence of film and TV and other entertainment formats, which has seen the company also embrace TV, podcasts and theater, while retaining its original mission of being a place that enables filmmakers to not just make their film, but to make the very best iteration of their film. “When we’re at our best, that’s exactly what we’re doing. It’s no more complicated than that. And when we are doing it, nothing feels more rewarding than doing that job well,” he said. Looking to near-term goals, Basner said the company was ramping up its productions in the arrival of former 20th Century Fox, DreamWorks and Universal Pictures exec Stacey Snider in the new role of Chief Creative Officer in January. “We are being more ambitious by investing more and making more films. This year we will make four films and a television series, and next year we already have four films in pre-production and hope to make another three,” said Basner. “The arrival of Snider as the Chief Creative Officer was an articulation of our desire to take more risk and to be more productive,” he continued. “Working with her these last nine months, you see this incredible creative talent, you see a skill set and a maturity that we don’t have ourselves, or that I don’t have myself, and it is definitely building confidence to invest further. But it’s really also, as she would say, it’s about making it better. The conversation that you had before: let’s take another look at this. Let’s do it a little bit better. That’s something she reminds me pretty much every day.” Jalen Brunson Brings Knicks To S52 Premiere; Trump & Zohran Mamdani In Cold Open ‘Star Wars’ Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend White House Blocks CNN, Networks Suspend Pool Coverage Read More About: Comments

title: Naomi Watts Talks Menopause – ‘I Was Crying in the Bathroom, Trying to Scratch Off My Estrogen Patch’ – Recalls Being Told She ‘Freaked People Out’ Early in Her Career: ‘Yeah, No Shit. I Was Desperate, Behind on My Rent and Getting Evicted’

I Was Desperate, Behind on My Rent and Getting Evicted’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Naomi Watts Talks Menopause – ‘I Was Crying in the Bathroom, Trying to Scratch Off My Estrogen Patch’ – Recalls Being Told She ‘Freaked People Out’ Early in Her Career: ‘Yeah, No Shit. I Was Desperate, Behind on My Rent and Getting Evicted’ 1 hour ago Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Courtesy of Andreas Rentz for Zurich Film Festival Naomi Watts waited a long time to become a star. “It was a grind. That 10 years before I met David, I became so locked up and I felt worthless. My agent pulled me aside and she said: ‘We need to have a heart to heart. Honey, you are too intense. You are freaking people out.’ I went: ‘Yeah, no shit.’ I was desperate! I was behind on my rent; I was getting evicted. I didn’t know what to bring to this room,” she recalled at Zurich Film Festival . Related Stories Taiwan Creative Content Fest Adds Spotlight Screenings to Court International Buyers “They told me I wasn’t funny last week, so now I am trying to be funny. They told me I wasn’t sexy – I’m trying to be sexy. You reshape yourself and try to read the tone of what is needed. That’s how it went and I couldn’t be myself anymore. I was either an extreme version of myself or a diluted version of myself. It took a genius like David Lynch to see beyond all that weirdness I built up, undo it and get to the real me.” Popular on Variety The resilience she built up from moving a lot as a kid was helpful, however. “You also have to know why you love it. Are you in it for the right reasons? My goal wasn’t just to be famous. I loved disappearing into these characters. I really cared and continued to investigate. I still do. There’s always more to learn.” Watts received the Golden Eye Award at Zurich Film Festival. During the ceremony, she also recalled these difficult first years of trying to become a successful actress, “which had a lot of dry spells.” “And then, mercifully, I met David Lynch in my late 20s and he changed my career.” “Mulholland Drive” is widely considered as her breakout. “That film gave me the most incredible role that affected people. To this day they still watch it. It’s still on these ‘bests’ lists. I’m just very, very proud to be a part of that film.” During the masterclass at the fest, Watts said she was also encouraged by Nicole Kidman. “She said: ‘All it takes is one thing, one thing could change everything. That didn’t make sense to me for a very long time. Until David Lynch, and then it became very real.” Right after “Mulholland Drive,” she starred in horror classic “The Ring.” “I tried to say ‘no.’ There’s no certainty to anything you do, ever,” she said. “My agents were excited about this. I said: ‘Wait. I just got this critical acclaim, so I want to instantly go into a Hollywood blockbuster-y movie?!’ I fought with my agent at the time. I didn’t know it was going to be a massive hit! I woke up the horror genre, in a way. It was a lucky, lucky break.” Watts also earned raves for “21 Grams” – “Extraordinary things can happen when you get tired and irritable from doing things too much,” she said, recalling that intense shoot. “If there’s any theme in my work, it’s grief. It’s why I do what I do: I’m trying to figure out the meaning of my life. Another one is identity. I love the story [that asks]: ‘Who are you?’ That also comes from my moving around as a kid. I was always on the outskirts of the group, trying to find my way in.” Watts’ recent role, in Ben Shirinian’s “The Housewife,” addresses that too. In the film, set in the 1960s, she plays a seemingly perfect housewife – but one who hides a terrible post-war past. “I never played a character like this, even though I look for flawed women and I’m not afraid of unlikeable. But this was extreme,” she said. She said: “I knew what I was stepping into. I knew it was going to be a daunting, haunting understanding. A character like that comes to you at night, in your dreams.” Ending the masterclass, Watts admitted it took her a while to stop focusing on other people’s opinions. “Vulnerability is a superpower. It has taken me a long time to know that, and own that. I wish I’d learn earlier on to be more myself and [care] less about pleasing people. Some people are born with that level of confidence – I was never that person.” “I still have a lot of self-doubt, but I don’t pretend it’s not a real thing. I try to see it as a gift. It’s more effective than just bullshitting your way through it all.” Being open about her hardships, as well as menopause, proved to be liberating, she said. “Menopause became a huge topic of conversation, because I went through it early on in my life and had no clue what was happening with my body. Once I talked about it with my partner, who is now my husband [actor Billy Crudup], and he was supportive, I went: ‘How about I just own the story?’ I’m in on the joke, although it’s not actually a joke. Why do we just suffer, instead of getting some normalcy? Just own it.” She recalled her first conversation about it with Crudup. “I was crying in the bathroom, trying to scratch off my estrogen patch. I told him what was going on, so nervous, and I thought: ‘He’s not gonna want to be with me anymore!’ He said: ‘Hold on. It’s great that you are taking care of yourself. Why are you ashamed?’ It was so sweet… And sexy. I felt safer than I ever felt.” She ended up founding Stripes Beauty, a brand designed for women navigating perimenopause and menopause. “Men have to be curious and compassionate. I Was Desperate, Behind on My Rent and Getting Evicted’ 1 hour ago Martin McDonagh Jokes About His Past – as a Hitman – and Calls ‘Wild Horse Nine’ His Most Political Film: ‘There’s Too Much Artistic Neutrality and Too Much Saying Nothing’ 2 hours ago Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Courtesy of Jonas Wiemann for Zurich Film Festival Martin McDonagh is taking a stand with “Wild Horse Nine.” “This is probably my most political film. That’s why I find it very exciting to be releasing this monster into the world,” he said at the Zurich Film Festival . “I feel like, in the modern day, there’s perhaps a little too much artistic neutrality, or too much saying nothing, not having an opinion or being apathetic. I’m excited to be doing the opposite with this one.” Related Stories Taiwan Creative Content Fest Adds Spotlight Screenings to Court International Buyers In his new black comedy, two CIA agents (played by John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) travel to Easter Island before the 1973 Chilean coup. However, it feels surprisingly timely. Popular on Variety “So many things in the present day mirror a lot of those types of interventions in the past. You can actually hear lines that I thought were about 1973 being interpreted by a modern audience as being about Venezuela a few months ago or other places around the world,” he noted. “The Russia jokes in the film are about their interventions in Finland 100 years ago, but we connect them to Ukraine now. I love that it has a resonance I wasn’t necessarily aware of in the writing of it.” McDonagh, who received A Tribute to… Award at the fest, looked back on his past during a masterclass. “I left school very young, at 16, and was unemployed for a long time. But with the hopes of being a writer. Part of that was not wanting to have a real job or a boss. That has remained with me until now,” he said. He wrote radio plays, all of which were rejected – “Mostly by the BBC. But I don’t bear a grudge” – and then became an acclaimed playwright. “As a film fan, I put all that into the energy of the plays. Things would happen that you wouldn’t usually see on stage. Like cats exploding [in ‘The Lieutenant of Inishmore’].” Seeing Al Pacino in “American Buffalo” by David Mamet was a pivotal moment. “I can still remember it to this day. He just came on stage and blew the whole theater away. It was this combination of a play, full of energy and swearing, amazing dialogue and this movie star who, well, you’d realize what acting really was when he was on stage.” McDonagh still writes “without the camera in mind,” but he enjoys the freedom of writing scripts. “It’s like when you don’t go to the gym for a long time; that’s where my theater brain is at the moment. But the muscle memory is still there.” The transition to cinema wasn’t exactly easy. “It was the bad rejections that really inspired me. Maybe I thrive not on encouragement, but anger,” he said. Still, his 2004 short “Six Shooter” won the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film. “It was probably the scariest situation I’ve been in artistically. But the wonderful thing was having Brendan Gleeson be part of it. He protected me from any interference. I couldn’t have done it without his help and guidance,” he recalled. He reunited with Gleeson on his hit “In Bruges,” also starring Colin Farrell, where two hitmen are forced to hide out after a mission gone wrong. “I used to be a hit man. People don’t know that. They thought it just was plays and then films. It was plays, killing and then films,” joked McDonagh. “I went to Bruges not knowing anything about it. I was supposed to meet a girl on the second night, and she didn’t turn up. It was this combination of thinking it was the most cinematic, undiscovered town I’d ever seen, and being bored as hell and just wanting to get drunk and get out of there.” Once again, he felt shielded by his lead actors. “Colin and Brendan were great partners in protecting me from any interference from the grown-ups. Who aren’t usually grown up; they’re children with a lot of money. It’s the nature of Hollywood,” he said. “I’m going to get in so much trouble. It’s good that it’s not being filmed, right?” McDonagh tackles serious – even shocking – topics in his films, yet somehow they still tend to be funny. But recently, he’s been noticing a change in his work. “I’ve tried to make sure that the films aren’t just about being cool. They’re about something deeper, and I guess more tragic. I’m leaving room for more contemplative scenes where the characters are on their own and it’s not funny. They’re left to think about their lives or dwell on their regrets.” This was the case with Frances McDormand, who played the grieving mother Mildred Hayes in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.” And now with John Malkovich in “ Wild Horse Nine .” “When they’re great actors like Frances or John, you see the sadness in their eyes, and you fill in what they’re thinking about. One of the ideas for John’s character was to give him the entire palette of emotions. You know that John can do comedy, he can do rage and he can do contemplative, quiet stuff. But I’m making sure all those things are together in one package,” he noted. “None of my films are sort of what I would call ‘Hollywood movies.’ They’re not simple, feel-good stories. When actors of that magnitude who have maybe done some of those films, and know they’re a little empty get to work on something different, it frees them up to show their brilliance.” McDonagh wouldn’t want to make bigger movies anyway. “Weirdly, I’m really happy with the trajectory or the level of films that I’ve made. I don’t want a bigger budget. I don’t even want more success. I just want to continue making films completely free from any interference from anyone. title: Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit Cinetic Launches Vertical Leap, Investment Vehicle & Producing Pathway For Pro Athletes — Zurich Summit One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? “We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don’t Need It” — Zurich Summit View All September 27, 2026 4:43am Hollywood sign Presley Ann / Getty Images At this weekend’s Zurich Summit a group of film financiers were asked by Deadline for their thoughts on the prospects of a U.S. federal film incentive. Last week, a bipartisan group of lawmakers unveiled the bill for a 20% incentive, which with bonuses could bring the total rebate to 30%. The move has long been called-for by the U.S. industry concerned by the exodus of production overseas. Alex Walton, former Co-Lead & Partner at WME Independent, told the Summit the move was “hugely positive”: “It’s wild to think there hasn’t been an efficient tax credit in America. It has helped many other countries. Spain is booming because of it now; and all over Europe. It’s going to take some time to be realized and for financial institutions to be able to cash flow it. But you’ve got to believe it will happen within the next three-four years, and then that will see all the foreign tax credits compete harder to maintain their positions.” Related Stories News "I Can Promise You, We Had No Idea That 'Obsession' Was Going To Become 'Obsession'", Says Hit Horror Film's Seller -- Zurich Summit Festivals 'Backrooms' Director Kane Parsons Says: "I Don't View It As A Horror Project" - Zurich Summit A start date is not yet set. The proposed text from last week stated that the credit would apply to qualifying film and TV productions beginning in taxable years after December 31, 2026 (effectively targeting projects starting in 2027). But bills can take years to pass. Watch on Deadline Andrea Scarso, Managing Partner at prolific financier IPR.VC, whose credits include Marty Supreme and Materialists , agreed that a U.S. incentive would be “positive” but also cautioned against rising production costs: “It remains to be seen whether the prices and budgets are also going up by the same amount, which is something that happens in some foreign territories when they increase the amount of tax credit or soft money. It’s always a balance. But overall, I think it’s good news.” Sarah Schweitzman, Co-Head CAA Media Finance, noted: “What’s important is that when you look at some of the international markets, you realize that we’re making movies there because of a tax incentive situation and I think if we’re able to federalize a tax incentive program in the U.S. it’s going to create many more jobs and invigorate crews, which is something we absolutely need in the U.S.” A recent Motion Picture Association study claimed that a federal film tax credit could increase U.S. production spending by $125BN and add more than 143,000 jobs by 2035. You can read more about the bill here . title: John Turturro on Joining the Oscar Race — and ‘Severance’ Season 3
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 27, 2026 3:39am John Turturro at the 22nd Zurich Film Festival Courtesy of Getty Hot on the heels of his Golden Eye award ceremony on Saturday night, John Turturro entertained another crowd at a Zurich Film Festival masterclass on Sunday. The Emmy-winning U.S. star has been recognized for his performance in Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , a project that is already garnering awards buzz . In the film, Turturro plays Harry, a seasoned pickpocket whose carefully controlled life is thrown into turmoil when a job goes wrong, setting off a tense chain of events that unfolds over the course of 36 hours. Related Stories TV Hints of 'Sex and the City' and 'Narcos': A Look at Literary Works Being Pitched for Screen Adaptations at Iberseries & Platino Industria Movies Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' Sweeps San Sebastian Awards as 'La Bola Negra,' 'NAZA' Earn Audience Nods In a career-spanning conversation with Deadline ‘s Melanie Goodfellow — the actor’s shining Golden Eye trophy neatly nestled between them — Turturro discussed growing up in an immigrant household, his decades-long friendship with Spike Lee, and the transition from acting to filmmaking. Turturro, who has steadily become one of the industry’s most formidable actors yet to put “Oscar nominee” on his resume, was asked about joining the best actor race this year with the Sundance success The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . “I never really have gone the whole hog with it,” he responded about the upcoming awards campaign. “But now I’m the lead in the film, so I’m going to support the film because I love the film.” He explained that being pulled into awards conversations is “helpful to help you do the next thing.” Turturro continued: “Is it nice to be acknowledged? Great, but that’s not why you do it. […] Just because a film is really popular doesn’t mean it will have staying power, but it’s nice to be in the conversation. I don’t look upon myself as being a competitive person. I’m competitive with myself,” he added. “I want to get the most out of what I can do, but it’s not sports!” However, he admitted to feeling surprised by the positive critic reaction out of Sundance. “Finally,” he thought, “I’m in something that people will see… My job is I like to try to improve, and I feel like being an actor is one of the few things you can improve in. You may not be able to run as fast as you did when you were younger, but I have a lot of life experience, and as you get older, you accumulate that, and you can distill things in a way that you couldn’t do when you were young, because you didn’t really experience all those things. And now I’ve experienced life, death, loss, being a parent, being married — what it is to really love someone versus falling in love. That’s a huge difference,” he giggled. Turturro regaled attendees with stories about his impressive stage career. He naturally came on to two major TV performances of his in the last decade: HBO’s The Night Of and Apple’s Severance . He coyly confirmed a return for his character, Irving Bailiff, in season three of the Emmy-winning Severance with Adam Scott. “Yeah,” he (eventually) told the room. “As long as they give me interesting things to do, then I’m interested.” He swiftly took the opportunity to gush over friend and colleague Christopher Walken, whose character, Burt Goodman, began a romance with Turturro’s Irving in season one. “‘Who’s going to be my love interest?'” Turturro asked before joining the show. “And they were like, ‘All these younger guys.’ I said, ‘Well no, I’ve worked with Chris Walken,’ and I said, ‘I want Chris, because I love Chris.’ And I don’t have to act that I love him because I love him.” Though Walken “didn’t understand a lot of the show,” Turturro was able to guide him through their authentic, real-life friendship. “I said, ‘Don’t worry about it. You just look at me.’ We have so much fun because I directed him like three times, and we’ve acted, and we’ve worked together a lot. And he’s a wonderful theater actor, and people obviously think he plays only strange [characters] but he can do a lot of different things. He’s also very sensitive, but he has a childlike joy in his work, and when that happens, anything is possible.” Turturro received a round of applause when discussing the HBO crime drama The Night Of , which ran for one season in 2016 and co-starred Riz Ahmed. It would later win five Emmys, and Turturro was nominated for his role as the eczema-stricken defense lawyer John Stone. “ The Night Of is something I’m very proud of,” said Turturro on Sunday. “It was originally a BBC thing, which I actually never watched because I didn’t want to be influenced.” He even confirmed that he actually wanted to do another season of it. “But they couldn’t agree on what the story would be,” revealed the actor. “But I loved doing it. It was one of those great experiences in my life.” Turturro’s career spans four decades, having worked with acclaimed directors such as Spike Lee, the Coen brothers, Martin Scorsese, Robert Redford, Robert De Niro, Nanni Moretti and Pedro Almodóvar. He first gained international recognition through his collaborations with Lee, appearing in Do the Right Thing and Jungle Fever . With Joel and Ethan Coen, he acted in Miller’s Crossing , Barton Fink , O Brother, Where Art Thou? and The Big Lebowksi , in which Turturro created the iconic Jesus Quintana. For his lead performance in Barton Fink , he won best actor at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival, an experience that Turturro reflected on at his Zurich masterclass. He even confessed to feeling like he lands “more normal” roles in Europe than across the Atlantic, and said he has turned down scripts “again and again” that involve his character being violent towards women. At his Zurich Golden Eye ceremony Saturday night, Turturro collected the award and quoted Italian novelist Cesare Pavese. “[He] once said that the only great thing in life is to begin. I still consider myself a beginner in many ways,” said the star. “I’m very fortunate. I wanted to make a living doing something that interested me and to do interesting work — to share that with an audience, [and that] wouldn’t diminish their intelligence at the same time,” he laughed. “I consider this an encouragement to continue.” Turturro joins 2026 Zurich honorees Julianne Moore and Tom Hiddleston . The 22nd edition runs Sept. 24-Oct. 4. THR

title: Beyond Frontman Doc ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ to Open U.K.’s Odyssey Film Festival, Lands Local Distribution (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 27, 2026 3:17am PT Beyond Frontman Doc ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ to Open U.K.’s Odyssey Film Festival, Lands Local Distribution (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Beyond Frontman Doc ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ to Open U.K.’s Odyssey Film Festival, Lands Local Distribution (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago ‘Hanuman Ansh’ Indian Sleeper Hit’s International Distribution Strategy Unveiled by ‘K.G.F,’ ‘Kantara’ Outfit Hombale Films (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Mizoguchi Retrospective, Anime Award Symposium and Teens Cinema Workshop Milestone 2 days ago See All Abnormal Studios “ Because of You Ka Kui ,” a documentary on the late Beyond frontman Wong Ka Kui, will open the sixth Odyssey Film Festival in the U.K., with NGO U.K.-China Film Collab also picking up the Hong Kong film for local distribution. Discussions began in March at FilMart in Hong Kong, which U.K.-China Film Collab attended with the U.K. Film Pavilion. The NGO deployed a similar approach last year with Robin Lee’s Hong Kong documentary “Four Trails,” which opened Odyssey and then played more widely in cinemas in 2025. Related Stories Taiwan Creative Content Fest Adds Spotlight Screenings to Court International Buyers The film, from Hong Kong director Rosa Pang, revisits Wong, the singer-songwriter who drove Beyond creatively and whose songs shaped a generation of Cantonese-speaking listeners in Hong Kong and further afield. The producers are Yip Sai Wing, one of Beyond’s founding members, and Leslie Chan, the manager who is credited with finding the group. Popular on Variety The film is built around interviews with people who knew Wong both personally and through work. These sit alongside rare concert recordings, never-before-shown archive material from his early years and footage that has not been released until now. It follows Wong from his first brushes with music through the rise of Beyond and his growth as a songwriter and performer, looking at his approach to music, his character and his ideals. Pang and Leslie Chan described it as a dedication to “a legend, an ordinary person, through memories of those who truly knew him. The film seeks to rediscover the real Wong Ka Kui.” Wong died in an accident in Japan in 1993, at age 31. The band’s songs have kept finding new listeners since. There is also a U.K. link. The film’s interview with Beyond founding member William Tang was shot in London. After an earlier theatrical run in Asia, “Because of You Ka Kui” will have its U.K. premiere as Odyssey’s opening film. The festival will run Sept. 28–Oct. 10 at a number of cinemas as well as online. Each edition is built around a different theme, and this year’s is #Fashion. “Beyond did not simply follow the fashion of their generation, in many ways, they helped create it, like Oasis for the U.K.,” said Hiu Man Chan, Odyssey’s artistic director and founder of U.K.-China Film Collab. “Their music, image, attitude and style became part of the cultural memory of Hong Kong and influenced generations across Asia. Fashion is not only about what an era wears; it is also about how a generation chooses to see and express itself. That makes ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ a very meaningful film to launch this year’s Odyssey.” Hiu Man Chan said the opening pick reflected the festival’s aim to treat fashion as more than clothing and catwalks, and to explore how film, music, visual identity and pop culture feed into one another. Bringing the film to the U.K. was “my true honor,” Hiu Man Chan added. The selection also stretches the fashion theme to cover youth culture and music. Beyond’s sound and look, which mixed international rock influences with a Hong Kong that was changing fast through the 1980s and early 1990s, became bound up with a generation of young fans. Yip has called the documentary a rare chance to find the “ordinary person” behind the bandleader and icon. Malaysian company Abnormal Studios launched “Because of You Ka Kui” internationally at FilMart in March, as the lead title of its new international sales arm. “‘Because of You Ka Kui’ is not about nostalgia. The honesty of Wong Ka Kui as a person – in what he thought, felt and believed – continues to resonate today,” Pang said. Leslie Chan said that after hearing all the interviews, “I really felt that I came to know Ka Kui all over again.” Odyssey’s sixth edition will program older films alongside new ones. The festival’s opening and some of its program have backing from the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London. title: Jia Zhangke Readies Zhao Tao Road Movie ‘Mamma Dunhuang,’ Rules Out AI in Production (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 27, 2026 2:19am PT Jia Zhangke Readies Zhao Tao Road Movie ‘Mamma Dunhuang,’ Rules Out AI in Production (EXCLUSIVE) By Jenny S. Li Plus Icon Jenny S. Li Latest AI Robots Dance in the Rain as Pingyao Film Festival Turns 10, Honors Ann Hui 3 days ago Chinese Feature ‘Big Little Things’ Turns a Real-Life Family Rift Into a Coming-Out Drama Now Headed for Venice Horizons (EXCLUSIVE) 4 weeks ago Shanghai Film Festival Takeaways: Debut Directors Rule the Golden Goblet While AI Remakes the Industry Around Them 3 months ago See All Pingyao International Film Festival Jia Zhangke will turn his attention to location scouting and production design for his next film, road movie “Mamma Dunhuang,” once the 10th Pingyao Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon International Film Festival wraps on Sept. 30. As revealed by Variety , the film follows a woman who drives from Dunhuang, in western China near Central Asia, all the way to the sea. It is set to shoot in early winter. Related Stories Taiwan Creative Content Fest Adds Spotlight Screenings to Court International Buyers “I really love western China, and I go to Dunhuang quite often. Dunhuang was a vital transit hub on the ancient Silk Road, keep going west and you can arrive in Rome. Yet, it is so far from the ocean,” Jia tells Variety . “So this whole film is a continental story that starts in Dunhuang and travels from the west to the eastern coastline – she drives until the sea comes into view.” Popular on Variety Zhao Tao, who won the David di Donatello Award for best actress for “Shun Li and the Poet,” will once again lead a Jia film, playing a homebound woman who uses AI to help her on the journey. “I will not use AI in making ‘Mamma Dunhuang,'” Jia says. “It only plays a role in the story.” Jia founded the Pingyao festival, which marks its 10th edition this year. He says that although it’s only been a decade, “the changes in the broader film ecosystem and the media landscape, as well as technological advancements, are drastic. Pingyao has remained nimble. We’ve been able to adapt continuously alongside the shifts in the film industry and surrounding media, capturing new developments for our curation. Looking ahead, I believe cinema will continue to evolve rapidly, so we will maintain this festival’s agility in the future. That very flexibility allows us to respond in real time to the most pressing cinematic and cultural topics on people’s minds today.” Jia wants Pingyao to remain a haven for cinephiles rather than a hall of fame. Where most international festivals program hundreds of films, he intends to keep Pingyao’s lineup lean, built around the year’s newest boutique titles, so the spotlight falls on the selected films and helps them reach the market. This year’s official program has just 51 films. “As a festival, not only must it have great programs, but also a vibe of equality, freedom, and ease, setting a tone where the filmmakers and audiences can merge together,” Jia says. “We put effort into bringing in films with great artistic value, and meanwhile cover as many countries and regions as possible, prioritizing regions less familiar to Chinese audiences, such as northeastern Europe and South America, hoping to introduce a broader spectrum of cinema to the Chinese audience.” Pingyao’s online ticketing system logged more than 70 million visits this year. Jia says part of the problem is Pingyao’s limited capacity, as the ancient city “is protected as a UNESCO World Heritage [Site]. We’ve been working on building one more theater, ideally inside the ancient city walls, with 300–500 seats to enlarge the capacity. But it is very difficult to realize this plan, we are still discussing.” For its fifth edition, the festival partnered with visual artist Xu Bing on “AI-IF,” a project that invited audiences to make films using AI. Jia says the festival’s AI projects have all been exhibitions, and none of this year’s official selections were made with AI. “We’ve been prudent,” Jia says. “But we maintain an open, observant, and inclusive stance toward AI. When it comes to technology advancement, each of us holds a different perspective, but there should be one fundamental attitude: we must understand and discuss it, not shy away from it. Pingyao upholds a spirit of prudent inclusivity.” Earlier this year, Jia created an AI-generated video . Jia also co-founded Unknown Pleasures , a Chinese art-house distributor named after his 2002 film, and says the company is negotiating to acquire two Cannes titles. In June, it announced deals for Russian auteur Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” and French cinematographer Marine Atlan’s debut feature “La Gradiva.” “We hope Unknown Pleasures’ acquired titles all have a great showcase in Pingyao,” Jia says. title: Hints of ‘Sex and the City’ and ‘Narcos’: A Look at Literary Works Being Pitched for Screen Adaptations at Iberseries & Platino Industria
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 27, 2026 1:00am The 16 titles featured in the inaugural Literary Works Pitch for Audiovisual Adaptation at Iberseries & Platino Industria Courtesy of Iberseries & Platino Industria If you need any proof of the potential for literary works from the Spanish-speaking world to be adapted for the screen, you need to look no further than YA bestseller author Mercedes Ron’s success with Prime Video and Banijay’s Pokeepsie Films production banner with the likes of the Fault trilogy and the recently launched Drawn Together . Literary Works Pitch for Audiovisual Adaptation, a new initiative developed by Iberseries & Platino Industria in collaboration with the Federation of Publishers Guilds of Spain (FGEE) and featured at this year’s sixth edition in Madrid running Sept. 29-Oct. 2, looks to connect publishers and literary agencies with production companies, streamers, studios and TV networks to feed their search for new intellectual properties. Related Stories Movies Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' Sweeps San Sebastian Awards as 'La Bola Negra,' 'NAZA' Earn Audience Nods Movies Zurich Summit Game Changer Glen Basner and Edward Berger Reminisce on a Wild 'Conclave' Ride Following a call for submissions, organizers selected 14 works from Spain and Mexico and one each from Germany and Argentina. The stories come from different genres, times and settings. Here is a look at the projects being pitched at Madrid: Alguien como tú by Xavier Bosch Agencia Literaria Antonia Kerrigan, Spain The Catalan author’s novel centers on an intense, cross-border affair between a married woman from Barcelona and an art gallery owner from Paris, with the woman’s daughter later trying to piece together details of the clandestine romance. Alka I. La mujer del infinito by Yaiza Nicolás Yaiza Nicolás, Spain The thriller-like adventure spanning three generations of women journeying through time revolves around a substance that prolongs youth and extends the boundaries of life. Así en la tierra como debajo de la tierra by Ana Paula Maia Scenic Rights, Spain A penal colony in a remote spot in Brazil is in its waning days, and its warden unleashes a horror scenario: every full moon, a selection of inmates is released, only to be hunted down with weapons. Cuando te atrevas a sentir by Tamara Molina Agencia Literaria Antonia Kerrigan, Spain Naila feels like a failure and has no clear goal in life. Bruno always succeeds and has a well-paying job that does not make him happy, but fears that quitting would make him a loser. But these two very different people may find comfort in each other. Cuando vi a la muerte prestar su sombrero by Rodrigo Unda Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial, Mexico This fantasy novel follows The Fates, living in the shadows with one job: guiding human souls to the afterlife. But one day, one of them suffers an injury, and she begins to experience human feelings. El sueño de las Mariposas by Cristina Atienza Cristina Atienza, Spain Mystery, history and memory collide by the sea in this novel about sisterhood. A woman’s interest in astrophysics and her defiance land her in confinement, with forced prayers and punishments. Las esposas del régimen by Miguel Ángel San Juan Alt Autores, Spain A modern mystery intersects with a historical look at women resisting General Franco’s patriarchal dictatorship in this novel, which pays tribute to silenced generations and warns against the return of oppressive ideologies. Masacre en el comedor by Ceferino Reato Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial, Mexico The journalist and political scientist investigates the deadliest guerrilla attack in 1970s Argentina, a Montoneros guerrilla group bombing at a Federal Police building during the country’s military dictatorship. Mentira by Care Santos Scenic Rights, Spain Xenia has had a reputation for getting the best grades and dreams of studying medicine. But then her academic performance suffers when she falls in love online. But who is the mysterious person she falls for, and are they real? Mi vida con él by Hilda Gadea Silvina Estévez, Argentina A film based on the memoirs of Hilda Gadea, the economist, intellectual, and activist who was Ernesto “Che” Guevara’s first wife, is already in the works. Nocturnos by Laura Pérez Alt Autores, Spain The writer and artist’s graphic novel uses a series of dreamlike vignettes to explore the mysterious and magical world of the night. You may not be aware yet, but you may well know Pérez’s work – she was nominated for an Emmy Award for her work on the opening title design for Only Murders in the Building . Too Match by Inma Benedito Agencia Literaria Dos Passos, Spain If you are looking for a contemporary story that has been described as a Madrid-style queer Sex and the City with less glamour, this one may be for you! This diary of failed dates is an ode to heartbreak. Una belleza terrible by José Ovejero Galaxia Gutenberg, Spain This biographical novel dives into the life and times of Leon Trotsky confidant Raymond Molinier (1904–1994), a chameleon-like figure who dedicated his life to revolutionary ideals and the workers’ struggle. Una casa llena de gente by Mariana Sández MertinWitt Literary Agency, Germany The debut novel explores family grief and trauma, generational friction, and memory through a narrative puzzle emerging from diaries and testimonies. Una Madre by Alejandro Palomas Scenic Rights, Spain Set on New Year’s Eve in a Barcelona apartment, the story sees Amalia, 65, fulfill her dream of gathering her whole family for a holiday dinner. It is a night of family and laughter, but also, through flashbacks, old secrets and hidden tensions. Vida y muerte del cartel de Medellín by Carlos Lehder Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial, Mexico If you loved Narcos , you may want to take a look at this one! After all, it is the memoir of a co-founder of the Medellín drug cartel in Colombia, detailing the criminal empire’s rise and fall. THR

Courtesy Everett Collection/Gilbert Flores/PMC After eight years and countless entries in the expanding onscreen universe, Star Wars is revisiting the Skywalker family with its next project. Deadline can confirm that Lucasfilm has tapped Skeleton Crew co-creator Jon Watts (director of Spider-Man: Homecoming , Spider-Man: Far From Home and Spider-Man: No Way Home ) to helm the first installment in a new trilogy of the Skywalker Saga, which is being penned by Simon Kinberg ( X-Men: Dark Phoenix , Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith ). Kinberg, who previously co-created the DisneyXD animated series Star Wars Rebels (2014-’18), has been working on the new trilogy since 2018, with Daisy Ridley reportedly eyed to reprise her role as Rey, as it will serve in the next chapter of the Skywalker Saga. Most recently, the franchise left off the Skywalker Saga with the latest trilogy, Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens (2015), Episode VIII — The Last Jedi (2017) and Episode IX — The Rise of Skywalker (2019), which was led by Ridley’s Rey. Since the last chapter in the Skywalker Saga, the Star Wars franchise has expanded with films and streaming series set throughout the onscreen universe, with the next installment Star Wars: Starfighter set for a May 28, 2027 premiere. Lucasfilm had no comment. Knight Edge Media was first to report the news. title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’
full_text: Sep 26, 2026 6:08pm PT ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’ By Antonio Ferme , Zack Sharf Getty Images for FLC “ Godzilla Minus Zero” blew the roof off Alice Tully Hall during its rapturous world premiere screening at the New York Film Festival . The long-awaited sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” earned rave first reactions from the press earlier in the day, and that adoration rolled right into the world premiere. The movie was met with multiple mid-screening applauses as the crowd went wild for all the kaiju mayhem on screen. Ahead of its debut later this year, “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” has been rated R for “violent content/bloody images,” making it the first entry in the 72-year-old franchise to receive an R-rating. Director Takashi Yamazaki , returning to helm the sequel after 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” became a roaring success, says securing the rating was “essential to the film.” “Logically, as a studio — and even as a director — you want as many people from the general public to be able to see your film,” Yamazaki told Variety at the premiere Saturday afternoon. “So, an R-rating might seem like a barrier to entry, and conversations about, ‘Hey, could we have not gotten this down to PG-13?’ of course are going to happen. In spite of that, though, there were certain scenes that, for me as a director, were so essential to the film. Censoring it or cutting it was just not an option for me.” Related Stories Taiwan Creative Content Fest Adds Spotlight Screenings to Court International Buyers Under MPA guidelines, viewers under 17 cannot attend an R-rated film without a parent or guardian, a restriction that has traditionally made the rating a commercial deterrent for studios releasing big-budget, four-quadrant films. That stigma has faded over the past decade, starting with the blockbuster success of 2016’s “Deadpool” ($782 million). In 2019, “Joker” ($1.07 billion) became the first R-rated film to cross the $1 billion threshold. That record was later broken by 2024’s “Deadpool & Wolverine” ($1.33 billion) — and more recently — 2026’s “The Odyssey” ($1.72 billion), which currently stands as the 17th highest-grossing film of all time worldwide. Popular on Variety “I think the R-rating, at one point, carried almost a negative connotation,” Yamazaki explained. “In more modern films, it actually creates a sort of expectation and excitement of, ‘Okay, well, they’re not censoring anything. The director and the cast’s voice is there, as is.’ So it is very encouraging to see other films who have preceded us that have already found a lot of success with the R-rating at the box office. Hopefully, we can continue that trend with ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.’” Inside the world premiere screening, New York Film Festival director Dennis Lim acknowledged that the Godzilla franchise might not be the first thing people think of playing at a major film festival. And yet, “We thought it was about time to bring a giant monster movie here.” Yamazaki took the stage to thunderous applause from the audience both before and after the screening, where he asked the crowd not to spoil any of the sequel’s many surprises on social media. “You are the first to see this film,” the filmmaker said. “There are a lot of ‘Godzilla’ fans around the world, so let’s work together and do not do any spoilers. No spoilers, please! I am trusting all of you guys.” Yamazaki also had the audience laughing while explaining how he never intended to create a sequel to “Godzilla Minus One.” Executives at Toho immediately started asking him about a follow-up movie once they saw the first cut of “Minus One,” a thought that made Yamazaki instantly nervous. It wasn’t until the movie opened in theaters and started to be celebrated around the world by audiences that the director realized a sequel would be a viable option. “Toho executives are here,” the director said. “With your reactions tonight I hope they don’t offer a third movie.” Sacha Baron Cohen to Star in Quentin Tarantino’s First Stage Play ‘The Popinjay Cavalier’ Squishmallows Movie in the Works at Amazon MGM (EXCLUSIVE) Ali G Movie Backlash Intensifies in the U.K. as Campaigners Try to Get Film Pulled From Cinemas Amazon Moves to Toss ‘Criminal’ Production Assistant’s Harassment Suit ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Trailer: Sacha Baron Cohen Returns as the London Bad Boy in New Amazon MGM Mockumentary Loading comments...

title: ‘Star Wars’: Jon Watts to Direct Next Movie for Lucasfilm
full_text: × Skip to main content By Borys Kit Plus Icon Borys Kit Senior Film Writer View All September 26, 2026 5:37pm Star Wars Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures/Photofest Logo text Even as Lucasfilm is deep in post-production on its next Star Wars movie, Star Wars: Starfighter , the next phase of a potential new Skywalker Saga is coming into focus. Jon Watts , the director behind a trio of Tom Holland Spider-Man movies, is now attached to direct the first installment of the Simon Kinberg -penned trilogy. It is a return to the franchise for Watts, who previously co-created Star Wars series Skeleton Crew in 2024. Kinberg has been working on writing a mystery trilogy since late 2024. The project is intended to act as the next chapter in what is referred to as the Skywalker Saga, the stories featuring the multi-generations of the Luke Skywalker family. The previous movies have been Episodes I through IX . The next one would be Episode X . Rey Skywalker, the Jedi played by Daisy Ridley in last trilogy released from 2015 and 2019, would appear in some capacity in the new trilogy. Related Stories Business Disney Seeking "Director of AI Enablement" After Warning of Layoffs Amid Companywide AI Push Movies Dolly Parton's '9 to 5' Comedy Returning to Theaters to Support Late Icon's Foundation Lucasfilm had no comment. Sources say the project is still in development and has not yet been greenlit by parent company Disney , although it seems to be project the furthest along the development track after Starfighter . Starfighter is being directed by Shawn Levy and stars Ryan Gosling. The movie is expected to hit theatres May 27, 2027, coinciding with the 50th anniversary of Star Wars . Watts is seen as a reliable choice for the franchise, which has occasionally, and would say famously, struggled with directors. After directing the indie thriller Cop Car , Watts was chosen by Marvel to helm the relaunch of the Spider-Man movies. The Tom Holland-starring movies, which included 2017’s Homecoming , 2019’s Far From Home , and 2021’s No Way Home , became progressively bigger productions and bigger hits at the box office. Watts proved he could navigate the complexities of massive big-budget productions. His post- Spider-Man work included the George Clooney-Brad Pitt-starring Wolfs , the high-profile misfire from Apple that upended its theatrical release and curiously announced a sequel that was never going to be made. Watts co-created and co-wrote Skeleton Crew , the well-regarded but unfortunately not greatly seen series that starred Jude Law and brought an Amblin vibe to the Star Wars universe. Watts directed two episodes of the show, which also had a starry assemblage of helmers that included David Lowery, Lee Isaac Chung, Jake Schreier, Bryce Dallas Howard, and the Daniels. title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Monster Movie Genius Takashi Yamazaki Returns With a Crackling Kaiju Epic Every Bit as Exciting as Its Predecessor
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 26, 2026 5:30pm 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Courtesy Everett Collection Writer, director and VFX wizard Takashi Yamazaki three years ago reinvigorated Japanese production titan Toho ’s seven-decade kaiju franchise with Godzilla Minus One , which delivered amply on monster mayhem with sophisticated (and Oscar-winning) effects, but perhaps more importantly, grounded the creature feature in affecting humanistic drama. By dividing the film’s attention between mass destruction and the raw pain of post-WWII trauma, reconstruction and societal reintegration — not to mention the atomic allegory — Yamazaki boldly reimagined the property while honoring the roots of the series’ 1954 original. Related Stories Movies James Gray on Broader Takeaways From Personal Film 'Paper Tiger': "What Connects Us Is What Matters" Movies 'Paper Tiger' Makes Its Case at NYFF Premiere: "A Labor of Love" That same meticulously balanced duality is evident in the director’s approach to the scaled-up sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero , an equally thrilling jolt of marauding monster action anchored by tender themes of family, friendship, camaraderie and personal courage. These are characters about whom we come to care deeply, and Yamazaki trusts his audience to know the value of time spent observing human relationships, ennobling the horror with tangible emotional stakes. Following its world premiere at the New York Film Festival , GKIDS will release the film in the U.S. Nov. 6. Godzilla Minus Zero The Bottom Line A radioactive blast. Venue : New York Film Festival (Spotlight Gala) Release date : Friday, Nov. 6 Cast : Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, Yuki Yamada, Kuranosuke Saski, Jun Kunimura, Mio Tanaka, Sakura Ando, Masami Nagasawa, Min Tanaka, Hidetaka Yoshioka Director-screenwriter : Takashi Yamazaki Rated R, 2 hours 15 minutes While the 1949 setting might be expected to make the aftermath of war recede into the past, it’s no less acutely felt here, with resonant moments touching on the complicated perceptions of the Japanese people toward America and the outsize impact on the rest of the world of its military industrial complex. World War II may be over, but its vicious cycle of loss, destruction and power-flexing continues. At the risk of angering the spoiler police — a cue to stop reading now if you’d rather go in blind — the new film ushers in another legendary kaiju first seen in 1964. Promotional materials for the most part refer evasively to “a new threat,” but fan anticipation and advance media have pretty much let the badass three-headed dragon out of the bag. Just as Japanese life appears to be returning to some kind of peacetime normalcy, with Godzilla exiled to the ocean depths and believed to have been killed in the previous movie, King Ghidorah comes swooping in with massive wings generating hurricane-force winds, ripping apart an entire town in the opening action. There’s a ton of sci-fi mythology in the Godzilla series concerning the origins of Ghidorah the Explorer, a creature at various times under the control of alien invaders and time-traveling human terrorists, which supposedly arrived on Earth inside a meteorite intent on detroying the planet, much as it had destroyed Venus thousands of years earlier. Yamazaki wisely ignores all that geek lore, instead treating the dragon as simply another killer Monsterverse freak with regenerative powers, inevitably destined to fight a death match with Godzilla for alpha status. Just as Godzilla can charge up his radioactive dorsal plates and shoot nuclear-level heat rays at his targets, Ghidorah has his own neat trick and three gaping fanged mouths with which to deploy it. The creature design is magnificent, with the huge wingspan and writhing tangle of elongated necks and tails cranking up the menace, while the ferociousness of the monster’s faces is enhanced to great effect by growling and roaring that can sound almost like an evil cackle. The mega-dragon spews out electromagnetic energy in the form of gravity beams; some of the most outstanding sequences involve those lightning-like bolts wrapping antigravitational forcefields around buildings, trains and anything else in Ghidorah’s path, sucked up into the air and then smashed to the ground for maximum wreckage. The heart of the previous film was former WWII kamikaze pilot Koichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) — stunned by the loss of his parents and crushed by guilt over his conduct in the dying days of the war — daring to dream of a life of domestic contentment only to see that dream repeatedly put in jeopardy. More or less given no choice, Koichi welcomed a young woman, Noriko (Minami Hamabe), into his home in the rubble of Tokyo, along with Akiko (adorable Sae Nagatani), the orphaned child she had found alone and terrified. Two years on, this found family are inextricably bound together, with flinty neighbor Sumiko (Sakura Ando, so memorable in Hirokazu Koreeda’s transcendent Shoplifters ), who also lost her family during the war, serving as “Auntie,” to lend a hand with Akiko. Once Ghidorah’s rampage spreads fresh terror, Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), the former naval weapons engineer now heading up the government’s Disaster Countermeasures Bureau, begins working on defense plans. He signs up his old comrades from the previous film along with a couple of new ones, meteorological forecaster Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa) and Professor Murakami (Min Tanaka), who lost his family in Hiroshima and may have a hidden agenda. Veteran Jun Kunimura (much better served here than in the Takashi Miike dud Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo ) also turns up as a doctor studying the effects of exposure to Godzilla’s cellular tissue on people involved in the attacks of Minus One . This phenomenon impacts Noriko, who miraculously survived the devastating Ginza attack last time around and has shown remarkable resilience, with her wounds healing at an uncanny rate. Yamazaki infuses tenderness into not just the core family but also the extended group, bound by profound fondness as much as by horrific shared experience. With Ghidorah dictating that the fight will now be airborne, Koichi is eager to get back in the pilot’s seat, compelled by a sense of duty to his country but also by lingering survivor’s guilt. Nodo wrestles with his own guilt over the countless deaths caused during the war by weapons he designed; he will not hear of Koichi putting his life at risk again and possibly robbing Akiko of a father. Nodo agrees only to bring the pilot on as an advisor, but Koichi is not easily deterred. The same goes for Noriko, whose medical condition may have the potential to be weaponized. Nodo and his crew set up a command center in Matsumoto City, where Aoyama determines that they can track Ghidorah as the creature responds to the electromagnetic force of a fast-moving storm system. Around this point Godzilla — fully regenerated and pissed as hell — resurfaces offshore. Given that heavy artillery and bombs have failed to slow down Ghidorah for long, Murakami calls Godzilla’s reappearance “divine providence,” insisting that setting the two monsters against each other is their only hope. Via some ingenious plotting, that entails a plan to lure the beasts into proximity, using a system tested by the professor in a cheeky homage to Hitchcock’s The Birds . The resulting clash of the legendary kaiju is a rip-roaring smackdown in a movie that keeps awing the audience with exhilarating action and then continually one-upping itself in the dustups that follow. I’m fairly sure I stopped breathing during a tense scene in which Godzilla bears down on a seaplane attempting a hurried liftoff. While Spider-Man: Brand New Day generated plenty of sparks and Dune 3 and Avengers: Doomsday are still to come, it’s interesting that some of the most pulse-pounding, intense and inventive action sequences on screens this year have been in two East Asian films — Godzilla Minus Zero and Hope . Stand down, Hollywood. As he demonstrated in Minus One , Yamazaki’s command of big-ass destruction spectacle is breathtaking, this time overseeing a significantly larger VFX team that makes the monsters not only mighty physical presences but also part of an immersive environment in which we experience the full force of their earth-shaking power. This is some of the most impressively seamless integration of major-scale CGI in recent memory. But the masterstroke of Yamazaki’s direction is the skill with which he ensures that the human drama remains no less compelling than the monster faceoffs. The film also benefits from initially making Godzilla the underdog in the fight, bringing back the creature’s representation in Japanese culture of nuclear trauma, natural disasters and the pervasively heavy anxiety that gripped the nation in the postwar years. Watching the Minus movies, you realize how much the lack of that cultural specificity limits the American Godzilla entries and how much these latest two Japanese films serve as a reclamation. While the action in those U.S. productions, notably Godzilla vs. Kong , can pack a visceral charge, the human element generally is forgettable and the mythology sketchy. But the characters here are richly developed, especially Koichi and Noriko, played with a mix of determination and vulnerability by Kamiki and Hamabe that fosters genuine emotional investment in them as both individuals and as a makeshift family; and the wonderful Yoshiyoka’s avuncular Noda, who has some of the film’s most affecting moments. As she was in the previous film, Ando’s hard-edged but soft-hearted Sumiko is a droll scene-stealer, and Nagasawa’s Aoyama is a terrific addition — it’s great to see a woman with authority and sharp intuition on the science team, even if she’s not immune to self-doubt. The first Japanese feature shot in IMAX, the movie looks stunning, with so much detail and nimble movement packed into returning DP Kozo Shibasaki’s frames. Period production design by Anri Jojo and Wataru Hirai is understated but evocative. And the score by another repeat collaborator, Naoki Sato, is a marvel, ranging from brooding apprehension, with solemn choral elements, to thunderous symphonic bursts for the big clashes. With the plot door open to another sequel, here’s hoping Yamazaki will keep on making new entries in this hugely entertaining series. And while we’re raiding the Toho kaiju vaults, bring back Mothra! Full credits Venue: New York Film Festival (Spotlight Gala) Release date: Friday, Nov. 6 Production companies: Toho Studios, Robot Communications Distribution: GKIDS Cast: Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, Yuki Yamada, Kuranosuke Saski, Jun Kunimura, Mio Tanaka, Sakura Ando, Masami Nagasawa, Min Tanaka, Hidetaka Yoshioka, Munetaka Aoki, Eita Okuno, Miou Tanaka, Sae Nagatani Director-screenwriter: Takashi Yamazaki Producers: Minami Ichikawa, Taichi Ueda, Kazuaki Kishida Executive producer: Hisashi Usui Director of photography: Kozo Shibasaki Production designers: Anri Jojo, Wataru Hirai Costume designer: Aiko Mizushima Music: Naoki Sato Editor: Ryuji Miyajima Sound: Hisafumi Takeuchi Visual effects: Takashi Yamazaki Visual effects supervisors: Takayuki Ueki, Elsin Okubo, Kiyoko Shibuya Casting: Toshie Tabata Rated R, 2 hours 15 minutes THR

title: Robert Eggers Wants To Do ‘Romeo & Juliet’ Because Things Got “So Dark” After ‘Werwulf’, Joking: “So, I’ll Do Something About Two Teenagers Killing Themselves”

title: James Gray on Broader Takeaways From Personal Film ‘Paper Tiger’: “What Connects Us Is What Matters”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All September 26, 2026 3:17pm From left: Roman Engel, Miles Teller, James Gray, Scarlett Johansson, Adam Driver and Gavin Goudey ahead of the North American premiere of 'Paper Tiger' at the 2026 NY Film Festival. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for FLC James Gray ‘s latest film Paper Tiger , like most of his work, draws from his personal and family history to tell a semi-fictionalized story of a Queens family in the 1980s that becomes entangled with the Russian mob, thanks to a moneymaking scheme pitched to patriarch Irwin ( Miles Teller ) by older brother Gary ( Adam Driver ). Coming after semi-autobiographical coming-of-age drama Armageddon Time , the crime thriller, Gray says, is not a sequel and doesn’t hew as closely to his own experience. “This one is much different. I think that one was much more close to the facts of the case,” Gray said after Paper Tiger ‘s North American premiere at the 2026 New York Film Festival of the differences between his latest film and Armageddon Time . “There are many things that my brother, I’m sure, will recognize as from our life, but it’s not a documentary. And I didn’t think it was a sequel. I wanted to make something kind of a little bit … Hitchcockian. … Pulpier is the wrong word, but a little bit more dramatically intense.” Related Stories Movies 'Paper Tiger' Makes Its Case at NYFF Premiere: "A Labor of Love" Movies New York Film Festival Kicks Off With James Gray, Tony Gilroy and Filmmakers Toast in New Lounge In addition to the thrills, Gray told THR before the Paper Tiger premiere that he’s hopeful audiences recognize the power of interpersonal relationships in the domestic drama. “I was trying to make a film in which the personal connection is everything, that love is everything,” Gray said. “Through that of course you want people to feel suspense and intensity and things that we love in a good drama, you hope. But then in the end, dare I use the word catharsis, what connects us is what matters. It’s almost a cautionary tale.” That broader human resonance is also reflected in the guidance Gray gave actor Roman Engel who plays the youngest of Irwin’s two sons, serving as somewhat of a stand-in for the director himself. “He would mostly just try to tell me to be myself on set and don’t try to live someone else’s experience, try to live your own and do the actions you would do while whatever’s happening to you,” Engel told THR of Gray’s direction. The film ends as Gary, Irwin and wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) are each dealing with their own personal issues and before they learn of each other’s fates, but Gray hopes that that lack of resolution allows the story to continue on beyond the bounds of the film. “I love the idea that the life of the movie goes on past the movie,” he said in a post-screening Q&A at the NY Film Festival Friday night . “I love the open ending. I love the idea that the film exists past the boundaries of the screen and the time. … With all of the characters, I wanted to make sure that there was a completion to their openness in a way, how open their characters were, and that nobody has the whole picture, because that’s like life, and it’s very untraditional actually for movies. Usually, in a movie somebody has the whole story.” Neon is set to release Paper Tiger in select U.S. theaters on Nov. 13, with a wider release on Nov. 20. THR

title: Sylvester Stallone Thought His Dad Would “Be Proud” To Make ‘Rocky’ Cameo: “It Got Really Nasty”
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Jalen Brunson’s Knicks Teammates Join Him During Opening Monologue ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story” View All September 26, 2026 3:10pm Sylvester Stallone and Burgess Meredith in 'Rocky' 1976 Courtesy Everett Collection As Sylvester Stallone made his breakout performance in Rocky , there was one person he couldn’t quite turn into a fan. While discussing his memoir The Steps , releasing Oct. 23, the 3x Oscar nominee recalled things on set getting “really nasty” after giving his real father Frank Stallone Sr. a cameo as the bell ringer in the 1976 boxing drama’s climactic match. “It was like: I just want you to love me for a little bit,” Sly explained to The New York Times . “Like, look what I did! Share it with me. I know you thought I was a fool my whole life, but here we are.” Related Stories Festivals ‘I Play Rocky’s Peter Farrelly Talks Why The Making Of ‘Rocky’ Was The Next Real-Life Story He Wanted To Take A Swing At – Toronto Studio Politics Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was “Impossible” But Was Appointed Anyway: “It Won’t Work” On the day of filming, Frank Sr. “didn’t ring the bell properly,” as his son “kept fighting and fighting and fighting. Everything’s choreographed. It’s one, two, three, four, bell. Not six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Carl Weathers is like, ‘What’s going on?'” Watch on Deadline Stallone continued, “And of course it ended up in an altercation by the end. It got really nasty. A really bad Italian drama. But for a moment I thought, Jesus, he’d be proud.” Sylvester Stallone in ‘Rocky’ (1976) Everett Collection In the interview, Stallone explained that his father “was very, very cold and tough” until they reconciled upon his death in 2011. “It would be these constant bombastic explosions and then total silence,” recalled Stallone of living alone with his dad. “If he and I were talking and I said, ‘I don’t know if I agree with that,’ he’d start spinning his fork and suck his teeth, and you knew what was coming. The next thing you know, wham! He had very big hands. You learn to duck. I didn’t put a lot of stuff in the book because I didn’t want a pity party, but it was insane.” In the biopic I Play Rocky , premiering Nov. 6 in theaters, Anthony Ippolito plays a young Stallone as he writes the first Rocky movie and fights to star as the titular boxer.
