title: Viral Lesbian Bar Article From Boston Globe Is Piquing Hollywood’s Interest
full_text: × Skip to main content By Aaron Couch Plus Icon Aaron Couch Film Editor View All September 26, 2026 2:54pm The former headquarters of the Boston Globe. Darren McCollester/Getty Images In the early 2000s, The Boston Globe published a series of bombshell articles that exposed the cover-up of abuse within the Catholic Archdiocese of Boston. The series was one of the more consequential pieces of journalism this century, winning a Pulitzer Prize and inspiring Spotlight , the 2015 film that won a best picture Oscar. Now, a very different Boston Globe piece has captured the zeitgeist — and Hollywood’s attention. The article in question is titled “A Western Mass. lesbian bar required KN-95 masks. When it changed the rules, all hell broke loose.” Related Stories Business UTA Signs the Kansas City Chiefs' Foolish Club Studios (Exclusive) Business UTA Boss Sends Companywide Memo Accusing Reporter of Unprofessional Bias The Sept. 22 article by Annalisa Quinn was all over social media feeds this week and quickly became one of the most read stories in Globe history. Now, insiders tell THR that UTA , which represents the Globe , has been fielding inquiries about potential adaptations for the article — both in the scripted space and the documentary sphere. Indeed, the article has several ready-made characters, from a besieged bar owner drowning in debt to former patrons furious that the bar has killed its mask policy — and who go above and beyond to let the owner know what they think. Articles are optioned all the time, of course, but only a select few make it to the screen, such as this weekend’s Robert Pattinson movie Primetime , which was based on a 2007 Esquire article . As sources involved in newspaper packages note, anything that gives your project a competitive edge is needed in this tough media landscape. “Everyone is scared, and nobody wants to make a decision,” notes one observer in this space. A project based on an article like this one? That could at least give a decision-maker the feeling they’ve got a safer bet. As for the Globe , a spokesperson tells THR, “This story has certainly resonated with a wide range of audiences nationally and internationally. It is now one of the most-read stories we’ve published, and has already garnered many thousands of subscriptions.” THR

title: Sylvester Stallone Says He Became Bulimic While Filming ‘Rocky’ Movies, Used Steroids
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 26, 2026 2:48pm Sylvester Stallone in 'Rocky V.' United Artists/Courtesy Everett Collection Sylvester Stallone is opening up about the extreme lengths he went to achieve his physique for the Rocky franchise. In a Saturday interview with the New York Times promoting his new memoir, The Steps , out Sept. 29, Stallone reflected on how his relationship with his body changed over the course of his career. During the height of the Rocky and Rambo franchises, the actor became known for his exceptionally muscular physique. “It became very intimate, you might say. It was my armor. I looked at Rocky: very smooth, very normal-looking guy. And then I said, I think the character would start to become a bit more vain. And then in Rambo, you’re playing a warrior, so you’d be a little bit more animalistic. You wouldn’t be so smooth,” he said. “I started to think: Design your body like a jaguar, a cat. Not big like Arnold [Schwarzenegger], but more feral and aggressive and very limber and athletic.” Related Stories Business Sylvester Stallone Learned About Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship While Watching TV: "It Won't Work" Movies 'I Play Rocky' Review: Anthony Ippolito Is an Endearing Pre-Stardom Sylvester Stallone in Peter Farrelly's Crowd-Pleasing Making-Of Drama But Stallone said it eventually became an obsession, leading him to develop bulimia while filming Rocky III . “Then it became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic. You heard it here first. I got down to 2.6 percent body fat when I was doing Rocky III, and I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing. And nobody does it without additives and drugs, period. I don’t care what they say.” When asked whether he was taking steroids to achieve his physique, Stallone confirmed that he was. “Oh, my God, you have to. But you do it in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off. People go, ‘Oh, you don’t get that way naturally.’ No, you don’t. But that also took a terrible toll,” he said. Stallone said his relationship with his physique began to shift when he took on a different kind of role in the 1997 film Cop Land . “It wasn’t until I did Cop Land, when I had to play the weakest guy in the room — partially deaf, overweight — that I felt somewhat liberated,” Stallone said. “Then things went sideways and I just fell out of grace with Hollywood. But yeah, I’ve abused my body. I’ve had nine back operations, two shoulder operations, three neck fusions. Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape.” Looking back, Stallone said he no longer views his physique as the armor it once was and wishes he had treated his body differently. “If I could do it over again, I would say, ‘Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts,'” he said. “I don’t know what it was about hurting myself all the time.” THR

title: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham Nearly Joins Oasis, But There’s Something A Bit Off About The Gallagher Brothers In ‘SNL UK’ Cold Open

SNL UK kicked off its Season 2 Episode 3 with new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, played by George Fouracres, returning to his beloved home of Manchester following a speech to the UN where he socked it to Russia, according to his good pal Angela Rayner (Celeste Dring). “I’m sick of Russia trying to divide the British people. We can divide ourselves thank you very much,” jokes Burnham. Before long, Oasis’ brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, played by Jack Shep and new cast member Freddie Meredith, arrive to offer Burnham the opportunity of a lifetime. Their guitarist has pulled out and Burnham, a guitar player himself, can step in. “Ange, cancel the budget I’m going on tour,” he tells Rayner.
